# Overview

`gpxtoolbox` can read GPS tracks from two file formats:

- **GPX** — the XML-based format used by many fitness apps and route planners.
- **FIT** — Garmin's binary format, used by Garmin devices and many other
  fitness devices.

Rather than remembering a different function for each format, the package
provides a single **unified interface** — `read_track()` and `analyse_track()` —
that detects the file format automatically and does the right thing.

This vignette shows how to use that unified interface, and explains the
FIT-specific setup and behaviours you should be aware of.

# Installation

Install the development version of `gpxtoolbox` from GitHub:

```r
# Install devtools if not already installed
install.packages("devtools")

# Install gpxtoolbox
devtools::install_github("martinctc/gpxtoolbox")
```

## FIT file support is optional

FIT support is provided through the `FITfileR` package. It is **not** installed
automatically with `gpxtoolbox`, because `FITfileR` is not on CRAN (it is
distributed primarily from GitHub). Install it separately if you need to read
FIT files:

```r
# Install FITfileR for FIT file support
remotes::install_github("grimbough/FITfileR")
```

If you only work with GPX files, you do not need `FITfileR` at all. Every GPX
feature of the package works without it.

# The unified track interface

Two functions form the unified interface:

| Function                   | Purpose                                                     |
|----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| `read_track(file_path)`    | Reads a `.gpx` or `.fit` file and returns the track points. |
| `analyse_track(file_path)` | Reads the file *and* calculates metrics and summary stats.  |

Format detection is based on the file extension:

- `.gpx` files are read with `read_gpx_track()`.
- `.fit` files are read with `read_fit_track()` (requires `FITfileR`).
- Any other extension raises an error.

The lower-level readers `read_gpx_track()` and `read_fit_track()` remain
available if you prefer to call them directly, and the original `analyse_gpx()`
still works — `analyse_gpx()` is now simply a wrapper around `analyse_track()`.

# Reading a GPX track

The package ships with an example GPX file. Reading it is identical to the FIT
workflow that follows — the only difference is the file you point at.

```{r}
library(gpxtoolbox)

# Path to the example GPX file bundled with the package
example_gpx_path <- system.file("extdata", "icc_intro_ride.gpx", package = "gpxtoolbox")

# read_track() detects the format from the .gpx extension
track_data <- read_track(example_gpx_path)

# Track points come back as a data frame of lon, lat, ele and time
head(track_data)
```

# Reading a FIT track

Reading a FIT file uses exactly the same function — just pass the path to a
`.fit` file. FIT files are typically exported from a Garmin device or synced
from a fitness platform.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Requires the FITfileR package (see Installation above)
fit_path <- "path/to/your_activity.fit"

fit_track <- read_track(fit_path)
head(fit_track)
```

If you prefer to be explicit, call the FIT reader directly:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit_track <- read_fit_track(fit_path)
```

Both produce the same four columns as GPX reading: `lon`, `lat`, `ele`, and
`time`.

## How FIT data is mapped

FIT files store their data as a series of *messages*. `read_fit_track()` reads
the `record` messages, which are the sequential points that make up a track, and
maps them onto the standard columns:

| FIT field        | Output column | Notes                                        |
|------------------|---------------|----------------------------------------------|
| `position_long`  | `lon`         | Converted to decimal degrees if needed.      |
| `position_lat`   | `lat`         | Converted to decimal degrees if needed.      |
| `altitude`       | `ele`         | `NA` when the file contains no altitude.     |
| `timestamp`      | `time`        | `POSIXct` in UTC.                            |

# FIT-specific behaviours

FIT files produced by different devices vary in what they contain. The reader
handles the common irregularities gracefully rather than failing:

- **Position sentinels.** Some devices write placeholder "sentinel" coordinates
  (for example `position_lat = 180`) for points with no fix. These are treated
  as missing and those rows are dropped, so a handful of bad points will not
  distort the whole track.
- **Missing elevation.** Many files (for example swim activities) record no
  altitude. Elevation is returned as `NA`, and the elevation range statistics
  (`max_elevation_m` and `min_elevation_m`) report `NA_real_` instead of
  `Inf`/`-Inf`.
- **Missing GPS fields entirely.** If a FIT file has `record` messages but no
  `position_lat`/`position_long` fields, reading stops with a message listing
  the missing fields.
- **No record messages.** If a FIT file contains no `record` messages at all
  (for example a monitoring file), reading stops with
  `"No record data found in FIT file. This may not be a valid GPS track file."`

# End-to-end analysis

`analyse_track()` bundles the whole workflow — read, calculate distance and
elevation, geocode key points, and summarise — into one call. It works with
either format.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Summary statistics for the example track
stats <- analyse_track(example_gpx_path)
print(stats)
```

This returns a named list including the total distance and elevation gain/loss,
plus the geocoded start, end, and 25%, 50%, and 75% points. (The chunk is not
run during the build because `analyse_track()` geocodes via an external API —
see the section "Identifying geographic locations" below. The sample GPX file
also has no timestamps, so the time-based fields `total_time_hours` and
`avg_speed` are omitted.)

The `return` argument controls what you get back:

- `"stats"` (default) — a named list of route statistics.
- `"data"` — the processed track points, with `cumulative_distance`,
  `ele_gain`/`ele_loss`, and a `location` column.
- `"plot"` — a visualisation of the route.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Processed track points, ready for your own analysis or plotting
processed <- analyse_track(example_gpx_path, return = "data")
head(processed)
```

The returned data frame keeps `lon`, `lat`, `ele`, and `time`, and adds
`distance`, `cumulative_distance`, `ele_gain`/`ele_loss`, the cumulative
elevation columns, and a `location` column.

## Plotting

`analyse_track(return = "plot")` accepts a `plot_mode`. Use `"ggplot"` (the
default) for static plots, or `"leaflet"` for an interactive map with markers.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Static ggplot2 route and elevation profile
analyse_track(example_gpx_path, return = "plot", plot_mode = "ggplot")

# Interactive leaflet map with route line and point markers
analyse_track(example_gpx_path, return = "plot", plot_mode = "leaflet")
```

You can also plot track points you have already read, using `plot_route()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
track_data <- read_track(example_gpx_path)
track_data <- calculate_distance(track_data)
plot_route(track_data, mode = "leaflet")
```

# Identifying geographic locations

`identify_geo()` reverse-geocodes track points via the OpenStreetMap Nominatim
API and adds a `location` column holding the full address string, for example
`"Highbury, London Borough of Islington, Greater London, England, United Kingdom"`.
`analyse_track()` calls it automatically, geocoding the start, end, and 25%,
50%, and 75% points. Use `all = TRUE` to geocode every point.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Identify locations for start, end, and key points (default)
track_data <- identify_geo(track_data)

# Or for every point — note this makes many more API calls
track_data <- identify_geo(track_data, all = TRUE)
```

This requires an active internet connection, and the Nominatim API is subject to
rate limits — prefer the default (`all = FALSE`) unless you really need every
point.

# Web links (GPX only)

`analyse_gpx()` and `analyse_track()` can accept a Strava or RideWithGPS route
link directly. The GPX file is downloaded to a temporary location and removed
afterwards. Web links are **GPX only** — FIT files must be local paths.

```r
# Analyse a route from a Strava link
stats <- analyse_track("https://www.strava.com/routes/3193200014155699162")

# Analyse a route from a RideWithGPS link
stats <- analyse_track("https://ridewithgps.com/routes/39294504")
```

# Troubleshooting

| Symptom                                                                       | Likely cause and fix                                              |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `"FITfileR package is required to read FIT files…"`                           | Install `FITfileR` from GitHub (see Installation).                |
| `"Missing required GPS fields in FIT file: …"`                                | The file has no position data; it is not a GPS track.             |
| `"No record data found in FIT file. This may not be a valid GPS track file."` | The file has no track records (e.g. a monitoring file).           |
| `"Unsupported file format: …"`                                                | `read_track()` only handles `.gpx` and `.fit`; check the extension. |
| Locations come back as `NA`                                                   | No internet connection, or the geocoding service was unavailable. |

# Conclusion

The unified interface means you rarely need to think about file formats:
`read_track()` and `analyse_track()` accept both GPX and FIT, detect the format
for you, and normalise the output to the same `lon`/`lat`/`ele`/`time` columns.
Install the optional `FITfileR` package when you need FIT support, and the rest
of the workflow — metrics, statistics, geocoding, and plots — works the same
either way.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
sessionInfo()
```
